planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or early fall into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, setting the root ball slightly high with a thick mulch of pine bark or leaf litter over the shallow roots.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or early fall into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, setting the root ball slightly high with a thick mulch of pine bark or leaf litter over the shallow roots. Choose a site in dappled woodland shade or a boggy edge where soil stays cool and evenly damp, since this species naturally grows in bog margins, wet thickets, and open coniferous woods across the northeastern United States and eastern Canada. In May, before its leaves fully expand, the low twiggy shrub covers itself in clusters of rosy-purple flowers with an unusual two-lipped shape. It is one of the hardiest and most cold-tolerant native azaleas and works well in a naturalized woodland or rain garden planting where taller shade trees keep the summer sun off its foliage.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in fall or early spring into loose, well-drained, acidic soil amended with leaf mold or conifer duff, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer.

directions: Set out container-grown plants in fall or early spring into loose, well-drained, acidic soil amended with leaf mold or conifer duff, and mulch to keep roots cool through summer. It grows naturally along streambanks and in open, partly shaded woods from California into southern Oregon, so give it filtered light beneath high canopy and steady moisture in its first few seasons while it establishes deep roots. Fragrant white to pale pink flowers with a yellow blotch open in early summer on a rangy, multi-stemmed shrub, and the scent carries well through a shaded border or informal woodland edge. Established plants tolerate summer drought better than most azaleas once their roots reach cooler subsoil.

planting.note: Transplant balled or container shrubs in fall into acidic, well-drained forest soil rich in organic matter, keeping the crown at grade and mulching with conifer needles or shredded bark.

directions: Transplant balled or container shrubs in fall into acidic, well-drained forest soil rich in organic matter, keeping the crown at grade and mulching with conifer needles or shredded bark. This is the dominant evergreen shrub layer beneath Douglas fir and redwood forests from British Columbia to California, so it thrives in dense to dappled shade and resents hot, exposed sites with reflected heat. Large trusses of pink to rosy-purple bell-shaped flowers appear in late spring above leathery, dark green leaves, giving structure and winter interest to a shaded native garden long after bloom. It is the state flower of Washington and pairs naturally with sword fern, salal, and huckleberry in a Pacific Northwest woodland planting.

planting.note: Plant in spring or early fall into moist, acidic, well-drained soil enriched with compost or leaf mold, siting it where dappled shade shields the flowers and foliage from harsh afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in spring or early fall into moist, acidic, well-drained soil enriched with compost or leaf mold, siting it where dappled shade shields the flowers and foliage from harsh afternoon sun. Native to the mountain woodlands of Korea, Manchuria, and Japan, it naturally grows as an understory shrub and performs best with morning sun and afternoon shelter from taller trees. In mid-spring, fragrant pale pink flowers open just as the whorled, obovate leaves emerge, and those same leaves often turn attractive shades of orange and red in fall, giving the shrub two strong seasons of interest. Its tiered branching habit and unusually large, rounded leaves make it a distinctive specimen for a woodland garden rather than just a spring-bloom shrub.

planting.note: Set out plants in spring into acidic, well-drained soil high in organic matter, watering deeply and mulching to conserve moisture while the shrub establishes.

directions: Set out plants in spring into acidic, well-drained soil high in organic matter, watering deeply and mulching to conserve moisture while the shrub establishes. Native to Korea, northeastern China, and Japan, it tolerates a range of light from partial shade to more open sites and is valued for blooming before almost any other woody plant in the garden, often while snow still lingers. Clouds of funnel-shaped rosy-lavender flowers cover the bare branches in very early spring, ahead of the leaves, making it a striking companion to snowdrops and early hellebores at the edge of a shaded border. It is one of the more cold-hardy deciduous rhododendrons and handles colder winters better than many broadleaf evergreen relatives.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs shallowly in spring or fall into acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and mulch lightly to keep the fibrous surface roots cool and moist.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs shallowly in spring or fall into acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter, and mulch lightly to keep the fibrous surface roots cool and moist. Native to the mountain summit of Yakushima Island in Japan, it grows naturally in a harsh, exposed habitat but has become a parent of countless compact hybrids because of its dense, mounded form and heavy woolly indumentum on the undersides of its leaves. Rounded trusses of pale pink flowers fading to white open in late spring against foliage that looks silvery and felted from below, giving the shrub interest even when not in bloom. Its naturally dwarf, tidy habit makes it useful in smaller shaded foundation plantings where larger rhododendron species would quickly outgrow the space.

planting.note: Plant in spring into moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with good drainage, positioning the shrub where it receives filtered light and shelter from strong midday sun.

directions: Plant in spring into moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with good drainage, positioning the shrub where it receives filtered light and shelter from strong midday sun. Native to the Caucasus region and parts of eastern Europe, it has long been grown as a parent species of the hardy Ghent azalea hybrids and thrives in the same open woodland conditions those hybrids prefer. In late spring, clusters of intensely fragrant golden-yellow flowers open before or with the emerging leaves, filling a shaded garden with scent that carries much farther than the plant's modest size would suggest. Its narrow, willow-like leaves often turn shades of red, purple, and orange in autumn, adding a second season of color to a woodland border.

planting.note: Divide clumps or set out plugs in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist soil, spacing plants to knit together into a low, textured groundcover over one or two seasons.

directions: Divide clumps or set out plugs in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist soil, spacing plants to knit together into a low, textured groundcover over one or two seasons. It occurs naturally in rich deciduous forests across eastern North America, tolerating deep shade and competition from tree roots better than most true grasses or sedges, and it spreads gradually by short rhizomes without becoming aggressive. Fine, grass-like leaves edged with soft white hairs form neat evergreen-to-semievergreen tufts, and small brownish flower clusters appear on wiry stems in mid-spring. Its fine texture and shade tolerance make it a useful low-maintenance filler between hostas, ferns, and other woodland perennials where turf grass will not grow.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall with the nose just below the soil surface into deep, moist, humus-rich soil, and mulch heavily since flowering-size bulbs take several years to build up before blooming.

directions: Plant bulbs in fall with the nose just below the soil surface into deep, moist, humus-rich soil, and mulch heavily since flowering-size bulbs take several years to build up before blooming. Native to shaded, moist mountain forests in central China, it needs the same cool, reliably damp woodland conditions as its larger relative Cardiocrinum giganteum and resents drying out or heavy midday sun. After several seasons of building a rosette of broad, heart-shaped leaves, a tall flowering stem finally emerges bearing pendant, trumpet-shaped white flowers streaked with maroon inside the throat in summer. The parent bulb dies after flowering but leaves offset bulbs behind, so a patch renews itself over time in an undisturbed shaded corner of the garden.
